europe.rationale: Facts: euro area flash HICP rose to 4.0% in October (energy +20.8%, core steady at 2.5%), the October composite PMI slowed to about 51.9 flash, and the BoE hiked 25bp to 4.0% on 5 Nov (8-1) with CPI projected near 5% in mid-2027 and a stated case for another rise. The offsets: TTF gas fell about 16% from its four-year high and Brent fell sharply on US-Iran diplomacy hopes after the US midterms. The STOXX 600 nearly hit a record on Thursday and finished the week only about 0.2% lower despite the US tech rout, with more than half of reporters beating Q3 estimates. Interpretation: the energy relief is real but rests on diplomacy (EU storage is about 74% full against an 86% five-year norm, and the Qatar force majeure runs to end-December), and hawkish ECB/BoE risk plus the Rheinmetall-led defence selloff balance it, so the net is neutral.

developed_ex_us.rationale: Facts: the main developed-market central banks outside the US are tightening against energy-driven inflation. The RBA hiked to 4.85% (6-3) on 3 Nov, the BoE to 4.0% on 5 Nov, and the BoC to 2.5% on 28 Oct. Canada lost 4,700 jobs in October as unemployment rose to 6.7%, its third straight month of job losses. The supports are that the dollar weakened after the US midterms (sterling's trade-weighted index is at its highest since June 2016), falling oil and gas prices ease the terms-of-trade squeeze for energy importers, and ex-US indices are less exposed to AI and held up better than the Nasdaq in the 5-6 Nov selloff. Interpretation: tightening into slowing growth roughly offsets currency and energy relief. Japan is outside this pillar, so confidence is low.

asia_dev_other.rationale: Facts: the RBA delivered its fifth hike of 2026 (to 4.85%), said inflation will not fall below 3% until late 2027, and flagged slowing output, falling house prices and rising unemployment. Singapore's DBS (net profit -5% y/y) and UOB both missed Q3 estimates, with net interest margins compressing, and all three Singapore bank stocks fell in results week. Hong Kong's Hang Seng rose 5.1% for the week, its best since March 2025, on China support measures, but fell 1.3% on Friday as the US AI selloff spread to Asia (Reuters). Interpretation: Australian tightening into a slowdown, softer Singapore bank earnings and AI-repricing risk for tech-heavy Asian developed markets outweigh the Hong Kong rebound, so this is a mild headwind. Korea and Taiwan were not researched in depth, so confidence is low.

regime_notes: The week turned on two US-driven shocks. First, the Democratic midterm sweep raised hopes for a US-Iran deal (Qatar is mediating), and Brent and TTF gas dropped sharply from their highs. That is the single biggest potential relief for Europe's energy-driven inflation (euro area HICP is at 4.0% with energy at +20.8%), but EU gas storage is only about 74% full and Qatari LNG remains under force majeure, so a breakdown in talks would quickly reverse the move. Second, the Nasdaq fell about 5.5% on 5 Nov on AI and antitrust repricing, and Europe and the other developed markets fell less because they hold less AI exposure. Central banks outside the US are hiking, not cutting: the BoE hiked to 4.0% (first rise since 2023), the RBA to 4.85% and the BoC to 2.5%, and the ECB held at 2.50% on 29 Oct with December live, so rate risk is a headwind for duration-sensitive sectors and for housing in Australia, the UK and Canada. A weaker dollar (sterling's trade-weighted index is at its highest since June 2016, and GBP/EUR is above 1.20) helps unhedged USD-based holders of European ETFs. European defence lost momentum after Rheinmetall's second guidance cut and the selloff on US defence-scrutiny worries.

red_flags.issue: Holding-level, not fund-level: Rheinmetall, a top weight in most European defence ETFs, cut its 2026 guidance for the second time and fell more than 17% on 5 Nov (down 48% YTD), and BAE, Leonardo and Saab also fell. Check each fund's concentration.
